exercices.enonce_intro_markdown:
**Paper 2 (2 hours 30 minutes).** This paper has three sections. Answer ALL eight questions: the four questions of Section A (10 marks each), the two questions of Section B (20 marks each) and the two questions of Section C (20 marks each). The total is 120 marks. In the examination itself, Section A offers five questions of which the best four are graded, and Section C offers three questions of which two are answered; this original paper contains only the questions to be answered. Show all the steps in your calculations. Useful data: molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. $=24000\ \text{cm}^3$; $1$ mole of electrons carries $96000\ \text{C}$. The relative atomic masses needed are given in the questions.

Boron exists as two isotopes, $^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}$ and $^{11}_{5}\mathrm{B}$. In a natural sample of boron, $20\%$ of the atoms are $^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}$ and $80\%$ are $^{11}_{5}\mathrm{B}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State the number of protons and the number of neutrons in an atom of $^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}$.

(ii) Explain why the two isotopes of boron have the same chemical properties.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The atomic number is the number of protons and the mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons. Chemical properties depend on the electrons, mainly the outer ones.

(i) The atomic number is $5$, so there are **5 protons**. The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number: $10-5=$ **5 neutrons**.

(ii) Both isotopes have $5$ protons, so a neutral atom of either has **5 electrons** with the same arrangement, $2, 3$. Chemical reactions involve the outer electrons, so the isotopes react in the same way. They differ only in the number of neutrons, which affects the mass and not the chemistry.

criteres_notation.libelle: You state $5$ protons
You state $5$ neutrons ($10-5$)
You explain that the isotopes have the same number of electrons, so the same outer electrons which decide the chemical properties

rappels_de_methode.competence: Atomic structure: particles, electron shells, ions and isotopes
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: The atomic number is the number of protons and the mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons. Chemical properties depend on the electrons, mainly the outer ones.

questions.enonce_markdown: Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron in this sample. Show your working.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The relative atomic mass is the average of the mass numbers of the isotopes, weighted by their percentages.

$$\text{RAM}=\frac{(20\times10)+(80\times11)}{100}=\frac{200+880}{100}=\frac{1080}{100}=10.8$$ The relative atomic mass of boron is **10.8**, closer to $11$ because most atoms are $^{11}\mathrm{B}$.

**Answer: $10.8$.**

### Piège à éviter
The answer must lie between $10$ and $11$, and nearer $11$ because $80\%$ of the atoms are $^{11}\mathrm{B}$; $10.5$ would be the simple mean.

criteres_notation.libelle: You use the abundances: $0.20\times10$ and $0.80\times11$
You add the two contributions: $2.0+8.8$
You obtain $10.8$

rappels_de_methode.competence: Atomic structure: particles, electron shells, ions and isotopes
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: The relative atomic mass is the average of the mass numbers of the isotopes, weighted by their percentages.

An element D has the electronic configuration $2, 8, 3$.

(i) State the group and the period of the Periodic Table to which D belongs.

(ii) Write the formula of the ion formed by D and give its electronic configuration.

(iii) The oxide of D reacts with both dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution. What name is given to an oxide with this behaviour?

### Rappel de méthode
The number of outer electrons gives the group and the number of occupied shells gives the period. A metal atom loses its outer electrons to form a positive ion.

(i) There are $3$ electrons in the outer shell, so D is in **Group III**; there are $3$ occupied shells, so it is in **Period 3**.

(ii) D loses its three outer electrons to form **$\mathrm{D^{3+}}$** with the configuration **$2, 8$**.

(iii) An oxide that reacts with both acids and alkalis is **amphoteric**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Name the catalyst used.

(ii) State the temperature and the pressure used in the process.

(iii) Explain why a high pressure is used.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
By Le Chatelier's principle an increase in pressure favours the side of the equation with fewer moles of gas.

(i) **Iron**.

(ii) About **$450\,^\circ\text{C}$** and about **$200$ atmospheres**.

(iii) The forward reaction changes $1+3=4$ moles of gas into $2$ moles of gas. A high pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, so the equilibrium moves to the right and more ammonia is formed. The rate is also higher.

### Piège à éviter
The catalyst does not change the yield; it only makes equilibrium arrive sooner.

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain why a temperature of about $450\,^\circ\text{C}$ is used rather than a much lower or a much higher temperature.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
For an exothermic reaction, a low temperature favours the products at equilibrium, but all reactions are slow when the temperature is low.

The forward reaction is **exothermic** ($\Delta H$ is negative), so a **low** temperature would give a **high yield** of ammonia. But at a low temperature the particles have less energy and the reaction is **too slow** to be useful. A **much higher** temperature would give a fast rate, but the equilibrium would move to the left and the **yield would be very low**. About $450\,^\circ\text{C}$ is a **compromise** that gives an acceptable rate and an acceptable yield.

criteres_notation.libelle: You say that a lower temperature gives a higher yield, because the forward reaction is exothermic, but the rate is too slow
You say that a higher temperature gives a faster rate but a lower yield
You conclude that $450\,^\circ\text{C}$ is a compromise between an acceptable rate and an acceptable yield

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: For an exothermic reaction, a low temperature favours the products at equilibrium, but all reactions are slow when the temperature is low.

exercices.enonce_intro_markdown: Copper is purified by electrolysis. The anode is a block of impure copper, the cathode is a thin sheet of pure copper, and the electrolyte is copper(II) sulphate solution.

questions.enonce_markdown: State which electrode is connected to the positive terminal of the supply and what happens to this electrode.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The electrode connected to the positive terminal is the anode. In this process the anode is made of the metal that is being purified.

The **impure copper anode** is connected to the positive terminal. It **dissolves** (becomes smaller): copper atoms lose electrons and go into the solution as copper(II) ions.

criteres_notation.libelle: You state that it is the anode, the block of impure copper
You state that it dissolves, because copper atoms change into copper(II) ions

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: The electrode connected to the positive terminal is the anode. In this process the anode is made of the metal that is being purified.

questions.enonce_markdown: Write the half-equation for the reaction at (i) the anode and (ii) the cathode, and state whether each reaction is oxidation or reduction.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Oxidation is loss of electrons and takes place at the anode; reduction is gain of electrons and takes place at the cathode.

(i) Anode: $\mathrm{Cu(s)\rightarrow Cu^{2+}(aq)+2e^-}$, **oxidation** (electrons are lost).

(ii) Cathode: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)+2e^-\rightarrow Cu(s)}$, **reduction** (electrons are gained).

criteres_notation.libelle: Anode: $\mathrm{Cu\rightarrow Cu^{2+}+2e^-}$
Cathode: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}+2e^-\rightarrow Cu}$
Anode is oxidation and cathode is reduction

rappels_de_methode.competence: Electrolysis: products at the electrodes, half-equations and calculations
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Oxidation is loss of electrons and takes place at the anode; reduction is gain of electrons and takes place at the cathode.

questions.enonce_markdown: A current of $2.0\ \text{A}$ flows for $30$ minutes. Calculate the mass of copper deposited on the cathode. (Cu = 64; $1$ mole of electrons carries $96000\ \text{C}$)
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Charge (coulombs) $=$ current (amperes) $\times$ time (seconds). The moles of electrons are the charge divided by $96000$, and copper(II) needs two electrons per atom.

$Q=It=2.0\times(30\times60)=3600\ \text{C}$. Moles of electrons $=\dfrac{3600}{96000}=0.0375\ \text{mol}$. Each copper atom needs $2$ electrons, so $n(\mathrm{Cu})=\dfrac{0.0375}{2}=0.01875\ \text{mol}$. Mass $=0.01875\times64=1.2\ \text{g}$.

**Answer: $1.2\ \text{g}$.**

### Piège à éviter
The time must be converted to seconds ($1800\ \text{s}$), and the moles of electrons divided by $2$.

criteres_notation.libelle: You calculate the charge: $2.0\times30\times60=3600\ \text{C}$
You calculate the moles of copper: $\dfrac{3600}{96000}\div2=0.01875\ \text{mol}$
You obtain $1.2\ \text{g}$

rappels_de_methode.competence: Electrolysis: products at the electrodes, half-equations and calculations
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Charge (coulombs) $=$ current (amperes) $\times$ time (seconds). The moles of electrons are the charge divided by $96000$, and copper(II) needs two electrons per atom.

questions.enonce_markdown: State and explain what happens to the concentration of copper(II) ions in the electrolyte during the electrolysis.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
In the purification of copper the same number of electrons is exchanged at both electrodes, so the number of ions removed equals the number of ions formed.

The concentration **stays the same**, so the blue colour of the solution does not fade. For every copper(II) ion that is deposited as copper at the cathode, one copper atom from the anode dissolves as a copper(II) ion, and the two changes happen at the same rate.

You explain that the copper(II) ions removed at the cathode are replaced by the copper that dissolves from the anode at the same rate

questions.enonce_markdown:
Hydrogen chloride is formed when hydrogen reacts with chlorine.

(i) State the type of bond in hydrogen chloride.

(ii) Describe how the bond is formed, in terms of the outer electrons of the two atoms.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A covalent bond forms between two non-metal atoms that share a pair of electrons so that each reaches a stable outer shell.

(i) The bond is **covalent**.

(ii) A hydrogen atom has $1$ outer electron and a chlorine atom has $7$. Each atom contributes **one electron to a shared pair**. Hydrogen then has $2$ electrons in its shell (a full first shell) and chlorine has $8$ (a full outer shell).

A metal conducts as a solid and as a liquid and can be hammered. Simple molecular substances have low melting points. A giant covalent substance has a very high melting point and does not conduct.

**J: giant metallic** (it conducts as a solid and as a liquid, and can be hammered into sheets). **K: simple molecular** (a low melting point of $-7\,^\circ\text{C}$, and it evaporates easily). **L: giant covalent** (a very high melting point, very hard, and no conduction).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Explain why J conducts electricity as a solid.

(ii) Explain why K has a low melting point.

(iii) Explain why L has a very high melting point.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Melting a simple molecular substance only needs the weak forces between molecules to be overcome; melting a giant covalent substance means breaking strong bonds throughout the lattice.

(i) In a metal the outer electrons are **delocalised**: they move freely through the lattice of positive ions and carry the current, even in the solid.

(ii) K is made of separate molecules. The **forces between the molecules are weak**, so little energy is needed to separate them. The covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken.

(iii) L is a **giant lattice of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds** in all directions. **A great deal of energy** is needed to break so many strong bonds.

(iii) You say that a lot of energy is needed to break these bonds

exercices.enonce_intro_markdown:
Two solids P and Q were examined. The tests and the observations are in the table.

| Test | Observation |
|---|---|
| **Solid P** (pale green crystals) was dissolved in distilled water to give a pale green solution, which was divided into two portions. | |
| P1: To the first portion, aqueous sodium hydroxide was added drop by drop and then in excess. | A green precipitate formed. It did not dissolve in excess. On standing in air, the precipitate turned brown. |
| P2: To the second portion, barium chloride solution was added, followed by dilute hydrochloric acid. | A white precipitate formed. It did not dissolve in the acid. |
| **Solid Q** (white powder). Q1: Q was heated strongly in a dry test tube. | A colourless gas that turned lime water milky was given off. The residue was yellow while hot and white when cold. |
| Q2: Q was added to dilute nitric acid. | Effervescence; Q dissolved to give a colourless solution, which was divided into two portions. |
| Q3: To the first portion, aqueous sodium hydroxide was added drop by drop and then in excess. | A white precipitate formed. It dissolved in excess to give a colourless solution. |
| Q4: To the second portion, aqueous ammonia was added drop by drop and then in excess. | A white precipitate formed. It dissolved in excess to give a colourless solution. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using tests P1 and P2:

(i) Identify the cation in P and state the observation that shows it.

(ii) Write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate in P1.

(iii) Identify the anion in P and write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate in P2.

(iv) Name P.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A green precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that turns brown in air shows iron(II) ions. A white precipitate with barium ions that is not dissolved by acid shows sulphate ions.

(i) The cation is **iron(II), $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$**: sodium hydroxide gives a **green precipitate that does not dissolve in excess and turns brown on standing**, because iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised to iron(III) hydroxide.

(ii) $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)\rightarrow Fe(OH)_2(s)}$.

(iii) The anion is **sulphate, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$**: barium chloride gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid (barium carbonate and barium sulphite would dissolve). $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow BaSO_4(s)}$.

(iv) P is **iron(II) sulphate**, $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$.

You write $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}+2OH^-\rightarrow Fe(OH)_2}$
You identify the sulphate ion
You write $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}+SO_4^{2-}\rightarrow BaSO_4}$
You name P as iron(II) sulphate

(ii) What does the colour of the residue in Q1 suggest about the cation in Q?

questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Carbonates give carbon dioxide with acids and on strong heating. Zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide and in excess ammonia; aluminium hydroxide dissolves only in excess sodium hydroxide.

(i) The gas that turns lime water milky is **carbon dioxide**, so the anion is the **carbonate ion, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$** (effervescence with dilute nitric acid confirms it).

(ii) Zinc oxide is **yellow when hot and white when cold**, so the residue suggests that Q contains **zinc**.

(iii) The cation is the **zinc ion, $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$**. Aluminium ions also give a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess, so Q3 does not separate $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ from $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$. In Q4 the precipitate **dissolves in excess ammonia**: aluminium hydroxide does not dissolve in excess ammonia, so the cation is $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$.

(iv) Q is **zinc carbonate**: $\mathrm{ZnCO_3(s)\rightarrow ZnO(s)+CO_2(g)}$.

You identify the anion as carbonate
You say the residue, yellow when hot and white when cold, is zinc oxide, which suggests zinc
You identify the cation as $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ and say that Q3 alone is not enough, because aluminium ions also give a white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide
You say that in Q4 the precipitate of aluminium hydroxide would NOT dissolve in excess ammonia, while that of zinc dissolves
You name Q as zinc carbonate and write $\mathrm{ZnCO_3\rightarrow ZnO+CO_2}$

A mass of $6.25\ \text{g}$ of Q is heated strongly until there is no further change. (Zn = 65, C = 12, O = 16; $1$ mole of gas occupies $24000\ \text{cm}^3$ at r.t.p.)

(i) Calculate the number of moles of Q.

(ii) Calculate the mass of the residue.

(iii) Calculate the volume of gas given off, measured at r.t.p.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Convert the mass to moles, use the ratio in the equation, then convert the moles of the product to a mass or a volume.

(i) $M(\mathrm{ZnCO_3})=65+12+3(16)=125\ \text{g/mol}$, so $n=\dfrac{6.25}{125}=0.050\ \text{mol}$.

(ii) $\mathrm{ZnCO_3\rightarrow ZnO+CO_2}$ is a $1:1:1$ ratio, so $n(\mathrm{ZnO})=0.050\ \text{mol}$. $M(\mathrm{ZnO})=65+16=81\ \text{g/mol}$, so the mass of residue $=0.050\times81=4.05\ \text{g}$.

(iii) $n(\mathrm{CO_2})=0.050\ \text{mol}$, so $V=0.050\times24000=1200\ \text{cm}^3$.

**Answer: $4.05\ \text{g}$ and $1200\ \text{cm}^3$.**

You use $M(\mathrm{ZnO})=81$
You obtain $4.05\ \text{g}$
You use the $1:1$ ratio for $\mathrm{CO_2}$
You obtain $1200\ \text{cm}^3$

Use the curve for Experiment 1 in Figure 2.

(i) At what time did the reaction stop?

(ii) Calculate the average rate of reaction during the first $40$ seconds, in $\text{cm}^3/\text{s}$.

(iii) Explain why the rate of reaction decreases as the reaction proceeds.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The average rate is the volume of gas formed divided by the time taken. On a volume-time graph the reaction is over when the curve becomes horizontal.

(i) The curve becomes horizontal at **$160\ \text{s}$**: no more gas is formed after that.

(ii) At $40\ \text{s}$ the volume is $60\ \text{cm}^3$, so the average rate is $\dfrac{60}{40}=1.5\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}$.

(iii) As the reaction proceeds the acid particles are used up and the marble chips become smaller, so the **concentration of the acid falls** and there are **fewer collisions per second** between the reacting particles. The curve becomes less steep.

**Answer: $160\ \text{s}$ and $1.5\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which curve in Figure 2 was obtained with the powdered marble? Explain why the powder reacts at a different rate, using the idea of colliding particles.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A reaction can only happen when particles collide. The rate increases when there are more collisions per second.

The powder gives **Experiment 2**, the steeper curve. A powder has a **much larger surface area** than chips of the same mass, so **more calcium carbonate particles are exposed** to the acid at the same time. The acid particles collide with calcium carbonate particles **more often**, so more successful collisions occur per second and the reaction is faster.

You say that the powder has a larger surface area
You say that more particles of calcium carbonate are exposed to the acid
You say that this gives more frequent collisions between particles, so a faster reaction

questions.enonce_markdown: Experiment 1 is repeated at $45\,^\circ\text{C}$ instead of $25\,^\circ\text{C}$. State two ways in which the curve would differ from the curve of Experiment 1, and explain the effect of the temperature on the rate.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A temperature rise increases the rate by increasing both the frequency of collisions and the proportion of collisions that have enough energy. It does not change the amount of product.

The curve would be **steeper**, reaching its maximum sooner, but it would level off at **the same final volume, $120\ \text{cm}^3$**, because the same mass of marble is used and the acid is in excess. At $45\,^\circ\text{C}$ the particles have **more kinetic energy and move faster**, so they collide **more often**. A **greater proportion of the collisions has energy equal to or greater than the activation energy**, so more of them lead to a reaction.

You say that more particles have an energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, so more collisions are successful

(The molar volume of a gas is $24000\ \text{cm}^3$ at r.t.p.; Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16.)

(i) Calculate the number of moles of carbon dioxide collected in Experiment 1.

(ii) Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate that reacted, and show that it agrees with the mass used.

(iii) The acid used was $25.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of hydrochloric acid of concentration $0.50\ \text{mol/dm}^3$. Show that the acid was in excess.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Moles of gas $=$ volume divided by the molar volume. The equation shows how many moles of each substance take part; a reagent is in excess when more of it is present than the equation requires.

(i) The final volume is $120\ \text{cm}^3$, so $n(\mathrm{CO_2})=\dfrac{120}{24000}=0.0050\ \text{mol}$.

(ii) The ratio $\mathrm{CaCO_3}:\mathrm{CO_2}$ is $1:1$, so $n(\mathrm{CaCO_3})=0.0050\ \text{mol}$. $M(\mathrm{CaCO_3})=100\ \text{g/mol}$, so the mass is $0.0050\times100=0.50\ \text{g}$. This is the mass of marble used, so **all the marble reacted**.

(iii) Acid available: $n(\mathrm{HCl})=0.50\times\dfrac{25.0}{1000}=0.0125\ \text{mol}$. Acid needed: $2\times0.0050=0.0100\ \text{mol}$. Since $0.0125>0.0100$, the **acid was in excess**.

**Answer: $0.0050\ \text{mol}$; $0.50\ \text{g}$; $0.0125\ \text{mol}$ against $0.0100\ \text{mol}$.**

Moles come from mass divided by molar mass; the equation then gives the moles of oxygen and of carbon dioxide, which are converted to a volume or a mass.
